extracted.intended_audience: Investigators preparing an NIH/NIAID resubmission (revise-and-resubmit) grant application
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for revising and resubmitting an NIH (NIAID) grant application after peer review, including rules, timing, how to address reviewer critiques, and tactical advice for a stronger resubmission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confirm NOFO validity and eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Check your original notice of funding opportunity (NOFO) to confirm it hasn't expired, you still meet eligibility requirements, and NIAID (or your chosen institute) still participates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the announcement has been reissued or updated, be aware of new deadlines, eligibility criteria, forms, and instructions that may have changed since your previous application. If you applied to a PA/PAS/PAR, you may resubmit to the same or different PA/PAS/PAR but still check the current NOFO for relevant details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide whether to wait for the summary statement
rubrics_metrics.description: You can begin revising before you receive your summary statement, but you must wait for the summary statement before you actually resubmit because you need it to discuss with your program officer and to address reviewers' feedback in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting revisions early can help meet the next receipt date, especially if you have new data, but you may need additional edits after seeing the summary statement. For new investigator R01s, summary statements may be prioritized and released earlier.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose study section path (same vs different)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether to revise and request the same study section or revise and request a different study section for review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Request the same study section when reviewers liked the idea and the issues are fixable. Consider a different study section if reviewers were not enthusiastic and the study section may have been a poor fit. Before requesting a different study section, evaluate reviewer expertise (using the roster), check reviewers' publications, consult colleagues/mentors, and remember participants rotate and NIH uses ad hoc reviewers. Regardless of the study section chosen, you must still address critiques from the original review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address all reviewers' comments
rubrics_metrics.description: You must address all the reviewers' points raised in the summary statement when preparing your resubmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss reviewers' points one by one; respond point-by-point when possible. Highlight reviewers' comments in the introduction and usually in the Research Plan so reviewers can see how you revised. If changes are extensive, explain them in the introduction only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the required introduction to summarize responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a one-page (unless exceptions apply) introduction that addresses all reviewers' issues stated in the summary statement and summarizes substantial additions, deletions, and changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exceptions: R25, Ts, Ds, and some K applications may allow a three-page introduction—always check funding opportunity instructions. Reviewers will look for their comments and check that you revised accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: One resubmission opportunity and timing limit
rubrics_metrics.description: You have only one opportunity to resubmit, and you must apply within 37 months of the original application's receipt date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because only one resubmission is allowed, do not resubmit until you can send the strongest possible application that effectively addresses all reviewers' comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow current NOFO forms and instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the forms from the most current notice of funding opportunity when preparing your resubmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scan the current NOFO for any changes. Even if you used older forms previously, the latest NOFO/forms prevail and may affect formatting, page limits, or instructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight and identify changes (marking changes optional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Summarize substantial scientific additions, deletions, and changes in the introduction; identifying individual changes in the application text is no longer required but is accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although marking changes by brackets, indents, or different typography in Specific Aims, Research Strategy, and attachments is optional, NIH will continue to accept applications that contain such mark-ups. Examples: applicants have used underlining or highlighting to show changes in sample resubmissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enhance the application beyond reviewer comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve any part of the application where possible, not only items raised by reviewers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add new preliminary data in the Preliminary Studies/Progress Report and strengthen sections reviewers did not question. You are not limited to revising only items mentioned in the summary statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond respectfully to critiques and explain disagreements
rubrics_metrics.description: Be respectful in tone even if you disagree with reviewers; if you disagree, explain why and provide supporting information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's better to change your proposal in response to critique where appropriate; if you insist on an approach, clearly justify it and provide additional data or rationale to support your position.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult program officer and institutional experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk with your program officer and institutional experts before deciding to resubmit and again after preparing the resubmission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program officers can advise on application changes, study section fit, timing, and whether to resubmit versus submit a new application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing strategy for resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider timing relative to receipt cycles, institute budgets, and lists for possible selective pay or end-of-year funding when planning to resubmit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If on a list for selective pay or end-of-year funding, resubmit rather than wait. However, don't rush—if you need more preliminary data, wait until you have it. Cycle-specific timing (e.g., Cycle 1 vs Cycle 3) can affect how long until an award.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider submitting a new application if science has evolved
rubrics_metrics.description: If a significant amount of time passes or the science has changed substantially, reassess whether to resubmit or submit a new application instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When major new data or substantial shifts in the field occur, a new application may be more appropriate than a resubmission that would require extensive changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expect uncertainty in reviewer behavior and outcomes
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand that reviewers may not be wedded to prior critiques, new reviewers may disagree or raise new issues, and the summary statement may not capture all concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many resubmissions improve in score, but there is no guarantee. If you have multiple active applications, eRA Commons will flag them (MAA) and NIH may fund an earlier application even if a resubmission scores worse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical advice for strengthening resubmission content
rubrics_metrics.description: Several tactical suggestions: capitalize on strengths, discard or revise weak parts, ensure Specific Aims align with hypotheses, and don't sacrifice important details to make space for responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If space is constrained, avoid dropping important methodological or conceptual details to make room for reviewer responses; instead restructure or strengthen the application where possible. Review sample successful resubmissions to see effective approaches to introductions and Research Strategy.
